content: Extracellular fluid (ECF) refers to all the body fluid that exists outside of cells. The fluid within cells is referred to as intracellular fluid. In mammals, including humans, the extracellular fluid is further divided into two primary compartments: interstitial fluid (ISF), which surrounds the cells, and blood plasma, which is the liquid component of blood. Additionally, extracellular fluid includes a smaller component known as transcellular fluid (TCF), which constitutes approximately 2.5% of the total ECF. In humans, the concentration of glucose in the extracellular fluid is maintained at approximately 5 millimoles per liter (mM) through homeostatic mechanisms. The pH of the extracellular fluid is tightly regulated by buffering systems to remain around 7.4, ensuring an optimal environment for cellular function. The total volume of extracellular fluid in the human body is typically about 15 liters, with 12 liters being interstitial fluid and 3 liters being plasma. The primary cations (positively charged ions) present in the extracellular fluid are sodium (at a concentration of approximately 140 mM), potassium (4 mM), and calcium (2 mM). The main anions (negatively charged ions) include chloride (110 mM) and hydrogen carbonate, also known as bicarbonate (26 mM). Compared to intracellular fluid, extracellular fluid contains significantly fewer proteins.
